newsitem.title: USA: State/local gov't groups map out federal agenda.
newsitem.headline: State/local gov't groups map out federal agenda.

text.p: A coalition of state and local government groups announced on Thursday a united federal agenda tackling issues such as transportation, the sale of radio frequencies, and the clean air act.

Nevada Gov. Bob Miller, chairman of the National Governors' Association, said the seven groups, meeting together for the first time in 10 years, would present a united front on a variety of federal issues that impact their governments.

"If past strategies perhaps have been a little divide and conquer the message we'd like to send to the inner beltway is we're together and we're together on some substantive issues and we're going to find even more issues we're together on," Miller said.

Miller said representatives of the groups took action at their meeting in Chicago to write a letter to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to extend the comment period for the Clean Air Act, which he said contains provisions that could have financial impact on state and local governments.

The groups also approved a letter to President Bill Clinton urging him to consider public safety needs before the federal government auctions off radio frequencies next year. Miller said he would deliver the letter at meeting with Clinton Friday.
Miller said the groups also reached some commonground on welfare reform, Medicaid and transportation reauthorization.

Jeff Wells, a Colorado state senator and chairman of the Council of State Governments, said with the reauthorization of the Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act of 1991 pending, the groups agreed to support a national transportation policy that would ensure the use of highway trust funds for transportation projects.

On the Medicaid front, Michael Box, Alabama House majority chairman and president of the National Conference of State Legislatures, said the groups want greater flexibility including the ability to implement managed care programs without having to seek federal waivers.
Another issue was the Internal Revenue Service's pursuit of yield-burning and the estimated $1 billion cost that could hit local governments.

Michael Schwartz, a Oklahoma City council member and president of the National League of Cities, said the coalition would submit comments on an IRS revenue procedure and would seek a meeting with a top U.S. Treasury official in an attempt to scuttle the procedure.

The IRS stunned the municipal bond market in July by announcing that issuers of advanced refunding bond can enter into "closing agreements" with the IRS to head off having the interest on their bonds declared taxable.
The action stemmed from allegations that underwriters overcharged some issuers for U.S. Treasuries bought in the open makret and used in bond refundings -- a practice dubbed yield burning.

The groups meeting in Chicago Thursday were the National League of Cities, National Governors' Association, National Conference of State Legislatures, Council of State Governments, National Association of Counties, U.S. Conference of Mayors and International City/County Management Association.
